SAN ANTONIO, Feb. 2-[Special. l-On
last Wednesday night, at the house OF
John McGraw, ten miles from Helena,
Karnes county, desperate shooting
ARRAY occurred, in which two brothers,
William and Eli Herrell, were killed
and Harry Patton mortally wounded. A
dance was going on, whisky was
plentiful and an argument between
Patton and one of the Harrells resulted
in drawing weapons. After the first
shot was fired the other Harrell took a
hand, and the ARRAY became general.
The room was small and crowded and
soon became too full of smoke to shoot,
and the firing ceased. Several others
were grazed, but not seriously hurt.

With murmurs soft as the wind-harp's sigh

There are few negroes In this country who

We see in this country comparatively few

Only along tho Niger River and Its great

BY far the larger part OF our African fel-

tho dense forests OF Senegambia, Liberia,
and Guinea, many also from tho low downs
aud lightly timbored region OF the lower
Congo, and q much smaller number from the
half sterile seaboard OF Portuguese Angola.
The furthest inland station OF white slave
dealers on tho Congo was at Bona, only
sixty-five miles from tho ocean, and the ter
ritory from which thoy filled their slave pens
extended inland only as far as Isangila,
STANLEYs second station, $50 miles from the
coast. The American slave trade, except in
the Niger basin. was traffic in coast ne

divided tho low-lying seaboard from the
plateaus Of Central Africa dwelt in compara-
two security, embarrassed by foreign men

people whom LIVINGSTONE and his sue
cessors have made known to tho world.


Thus, according to the testimony OF nll
travellers, our colored neighbors are. for the
most part, derived from the least Intelligent
and the most unfortunate OF tho African
races. Tho subdivisions OF the Bantu family,
from the Niam-Niams north OF the equator
to tho Kalllrs OF the southern coast are
quito distinct In their physical mental, and
social development from the true negro.
Tho Congo explorers tell US that tho higher

type becomes. The average coast negro,
with his ill-shaped figure splHy feet. smooth.
retreating chin blubber lips, and woolly head,

Bantu, 4 who Is pictured to US as tall

CEREDO, w. VA, April 25-A double tragedy
occurred about nine miles from this place on
the Ohio side, Thursday night, the result of a
lovers quarrel. Early In the evening Thomas
Wilson called on Miss Minnie Jacobs, his sweet
heart. Shortly afterward another suitor for
Miss Jacobs hand arrived at the house. Wilson
became jealous, and said something to the girl
which she resented. A quarrel ensued, In
which Hefner' the second suitor took part.
Finally Wilson drew . revolver and fired quick
ly at Hefner, but the ball struck Miss Jacobs,
who was standing near him. A second shot
struck Hefner In the breast. Both the wounded
people lived an hour after the shooting. Wilson
ded and has not yet been arrested.

CHICAGO, December Probably the


most exciting glove contest ever wit


messed in Chicago occurred here tonight


in which Jack Burke, of Chicago, in


three rounds knocked out Mike Cleary,
of New York. As early MS 1880 O'Clock
tonight the atmosphere of Battery d.
exhaled by fully 1000 pairs Of lungs,
reeked with cigar smoke, and the mob
not only packed the building but ran
over into the street. Ii was nearly 10

made their appearance and the crowd
proceeded to cheer itself hoarse. Pro-
tessor Tom Chandler, Of Boston, and
Captain Dalton. Of Chicago. seconded
Cleary, while Tom Chandler. Of Chicago,
and Jack Floto performed the same SER
vice for Burke. Both men were in fine
condition, Burke tipping the scales at l65
and Cleary about the same. The men
spared an instant for an opening and
moment later Cleary went to grass from
a terrific back handler from Burke's left,
which struck him square in the eye and
brought the blood. The round finished
with some Intellectual attempts on
Cleary's part to get in his right ON
Burke's face.


The second round panned out rather
favorably for Cleary. who got in sting
ing counters with his left on Burke's
cheek. Cleary tapped Burke gently
twice more and the round closed with
cautious sparring on both sides.


When the men stood up for the third
round Barkes pink and glowing
skin showed in strange contrast
to the almost marble whiteness
of Cleary's fine face and physique.
Burke's whole aspect was eloquent OF
yigor and confidence. yet Cleary, bale
and supple, looked well his match. The
New Yorker began to force the fighting
but Burke impetuously forced him into
the corner, hit two rattling blows on the
face with his left, then parrying Cleary's
right with his own right glove, struck
the New Yorker heavily on the neck
Cleary staggered and seemed dazed for
moment, then he recovered himself
with an effort and forced Burke desper-
ately to the opposite side of the ring.
Cleary was breathing heavily and
shook slightly with suppressed ex-
citement, while Burke was perfectly
cool and collected, watched calmly for
his chance. II came and quick as
flash his right arm shot out and Cleary
fell like log The blow caught him
fairly just under and behind the left ear
and knocked him senseless. 'My God
he has killed him, some one muttered
and the huge audience became perfectly
silent. Burke stepped to where his
fallen adversary lay stretched out at full
length on his back. The victor his face
exhibiting genuine alarm, stopped over
Cleary and shook him gently. A little
later Cleary's PROSTATE form showed
signs OF life and the crowd rose with
wild cries of "BErke Burke !"


The champion climbed over the repes
and walked jauntily to his dressing
room. Cleary's seconds picked him up
and helped him to his dressing room,
where he revived in few minutes.
Since Burke went to California after his
set-to with Sullivan, he has cultivated
the offensive use of lis right hand.
which is believed by many to be the Sc
cret OF his remarkable succesJ tonight.

The silent sympathy of love


To me is dearer now than praise.

My hearth and heart keep open room,


Come smiling through the shadows long,
Be with me while the sun goes down,
And with your cheerful voices drown


The minor of my evening song.

The wise eternal oversight,


And love, and power, and righteous will
Remain the law of destiny
The best for each and all must be,

NEW Y"RK, Sept 5.-A Madrid dispatch has
the following: Last night official dispatches
reached the government from the Philippines
stating that German gunboat landed troops
on the night of the oath of August at zap
island and hoisted the German flag there. The
Spanish vessels, San Quentin and Manila were
at zap bay at the time. The captains
of the Spanish vessels and the Spanish
governor-since dismissed by telegraph-pro-
tested with energy against the occupation. The
Spanish gunboaLs cleared decks for action and
the Manila was about to open fire upon the Ger
man gunboat, when she was signalled to desist
which she did most reluctantly. third Span
ish vessel, the Nelastoro, has arrived at zap
bay This news causes the widest
excitement throughout Spain. Crowds
gathered in the streets of Madrid all
night long, frantically gesticulating
and calling the Emperor William, the Crown
Prince and Bismarck the vilest names. Several
thousand people, shouting "Death to Bismarck"
and viva Espana," mobbed the German en-
bassy building, smashing the windows, break
ing into . thousand pieces the German arms on
the building and trampling the fragments un-
der their feet. The embassy was completely
mObbed. The furniture and mirrors were
dashed to pieces the people almost foaming at
their mouths with frenzy. The king will arrive
here to-day. Several of the soberest Spaniards
feel confident that the affair must now end

in large forces to indulge in the annual custom

charges. Many brought their lunches with them

high.water pants and shirt sleeves he rolled
eggs, rolled himself and rolled other boys, and
virtually took possession of the grounds. Presi-
dent Cleveland, now and then, had an opportu-
nifty during the day to glance from his library
windows at the merry throng, and in witness
ing the enjoyment the little ones took in their
sports, which were new to him, must have felt
well repaid for not forbidding them from tres
passing upon. their Easter play grounds.

Sweet Air, 10th District.-From the wintry
surroundings of snow and ice, leafess trees and
chilling winds, one can hardly believe the depar-
ture of the bitter season is at hand AT least this
breezy month will have its sway before gentle
spring, and then look out for buds and blossoms
and busy times. Even now "coming events cast
their shadows;" seeds being carefully selected
and assorted, implements sharpened and cleaned,
calculations planned and devised, and everything
in readiness for the temperance of the prophetic
ground hog.


The weather has been remarkably severe and
the principal damage done thereby will be felt in
t. wheat crop. This apparently is the general
complaint, although there few exceptions.


How very mistaken would great many be who
think there is nothing to dc in the country during
the winter months. Why, there is seldom an idle
moment, save in the evening or when the storm is
unusually severe. Just at present the all impor
tant work is log hauling and building. Smoke
houses, sheds and outbuildings of every descrip-
ton are springing up like mushrooms, and every
preparation for the approaching season. But the
birds, with iron like persistency, chirp and
linger with determination that means the snow
flakes have not all been spent.

A difficulty occurred between Bill Moss and
John and Eliza Cook Thursday night. Moss shot
John Cook through the bowels killing him, and
also shot Eliza Cook in the right breast, in
hicting probably fatal wound. Moss escaped

into the woods and overlook him. He turned
and fired twice at the dogs killing one of them.

Adispatch from Standing Rock Indian Agency,
Dakota, conveys the interesting intelligence
that Stanley Huntley, author Of the famous
''Spoopendyke' papers, at one time connected
with the Dakota PRESS later Of Washington and
now of Brooklyn, through the recent death Of
Young Antelope, becomes chief Of the Peton ma

ago, when the United States troops were in pur-

Sioux chief at distance OF several hundred
miles, without the aid of a telephone. Tired of
securing the plains, Huntley crossed the border
and became the guest of Major Walsh at Wood
Mountain, in British Northwest Territory. Here,
camped around the Majors post, were old men
and squaws, among whom were Little Knife,
hereditary chieftain Of the Tetons, who was too

jured his leg, and the medicine men failed to

up to die. Huntley, with newspaper mans
extensive knowledge, bound the wound with
leaves and oil, and Little Knife recovered.

Bull ana bis troupe were East an adopted sister
of HuntleY's was with them and recognized
Huntley. Little Knife had two sons, Mountain
Bull and Young Antelope. The former was
killed some time ago. and now By Antelspe's
death Huntley becomes chief az male relation
by adoption, this tie being as strong as blood
among the Indians. Huntley's Indian name ID

text:
Miss Mary Conkling, the sister of
Hon. Roscoe Conkling, whose death
recently occurred at Rochester, pos
sessed in a marked degree the charac-
teristics of the Conkling family, which
were SO clearly defined by her father,
Judge Conkling, and her illustrious
brother, Roscoe. She was a brilliant
conversationalist, but was much better
talker than listener, because she pos
sessed remarkably fastidious tastes and
would not allow herself to hear conver-
sation upon topics that in any way con-
hicted with her elevated notion of pro-
priety. Her language was always care
fully chosen from the choicest words
and her high moral sense cropped out
in every discussion to which she was
party. More than one of her Roches-
ter friends have, however, felt the keen.
edge of her sarcasm, which, like that of
her brother Roscoe, was always digni-
fed and couched in language that made
it cut deeper the longer it was thought
over. She was always remarkably cool
and dispassionate, even when engaged
in conversations with people who ad
vanced opinions in opposition to hers.
At such times she would descend from
the lofty plain of her argument long
enough to make single remark, which,
like sugar coated pill, seemed at
first to be very harmless, but which,
under analysis, was found to possess
the very sharpest of sarcasm. In her
personal habits she to remarkable ex-
tent emphasized her fastidiousness and
vanity.


An instance showing how particular
she was occurred while she was at the
City Hospital. She wore a wig and
false teeth, and she would never con-
sent, even when very i'll and weak, to
allow her physician to enter her room
until she had adjusted these and peeped
in the mirror to satisfy herself that she
was presentable. During her last ill
ness the same spirit ruled her to such an
extent that she would not even allow
her nurse to bathe her. When she was
unable to leave her bed she would have
the preparations all made and then dis
miss her nurse, while she, alone and un-
aided, performed such ablutions as her
strength would permit. Although the
wig she wore was so perfectly made that
but few could detect it from her own
hair, she had a new one made some
time before her decease and exacted
promise from her hair-dresser that she
would see that the new wig was used
when the undertaken placed her in the
casket. The most striking instance of
her extreme sense of etiquette occurred
but few months before her death. AT
the house of her most intimate friend
in the city she saw book she wished
to read and asked if she could take it to
her room. Permission was given and
the book was handed her to take away.
For several weeks she did not call on
her friend, who could not imagine what
she had done to wound Miss Conkling's
feelings. From third lady she subSe-
quently learned that Miss Conkling's
reason for not calling was that the book
was handed to her without an outer
covering and that she supposed from
that her presence was not wanted.
The lady had no such idea and was sur
prised to hear that Miss Conkling so
considered if.
